series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/8] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch detects and handles zonelist rebuilds caused by memory hot-add, which can lead to spurious allocation failures for __GFP_THISNODE callers. The issue arises when onlining a zone's first block rewrites the zonelists in place, causing intermediate list states that can be observed by concurrent allocations. To fix this, the patch gates sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers all configurations that rebuild zonelists after boot. This change ensures that allocation failures are avoided even when memory is being added to a node.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/8] mm/page_alloc: snapshot the preferred zone against shrink rebuilds
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug by reading the preferred zone only once in the get_page_from_freelist function, rather than re-reading it at every use. This is necessary because concurrent zonelist rebuilds can null or replace the preferred zone slot. The patch ensures that a stale but valid zone is used instead of causing a crash.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/8] mm/mmzone: read each zoneref slot once when filtering by nodemask
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug by reading each zoneref slot only once when filtering by nodemask. The problem occurred because the code was reading the same slot twice, which could return a NULL zone after offlining its last block. This caused a crash when trying to access the node of a NULL zone. The patch fixes this issue by testing the zone directly in the first read and returning immediately if it's NULL.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/8] mm/page_alloc: pass the zone, not the zoneref, to reclaim_retry_zone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug by passing the zone to the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint instead of the zoneref. The bug occurs when offlining a zone's last block rebuilds the zonelists in place, causing the shrunk list's NULL terminator to land on the slot being read. The patch changes the tracepoint to use the already loaded zone from the loop, which fixes the issue and prevents kernel oopses.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 5/8] mm/page_alloc: retry allocations that raced with a zonelist rebuild
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a race condition between GFP_KERNEL allocations and zonelist rebuilds in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism. When a zone is rebuilt, its position in the zonelist can change, potentially causing an allocation to land in a different zone than intended. The patch introduces a check that retries allocations if they have landed in a zone that has been rebuilt since the allocation was initiated. This ensures that the allocation is retried with the correct zone index and node. The patch also adds a new function to sample the zonelist update sequence count without waiting for a writer, which is used by the fast and bulk paths to detect changes to the zonelist.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 6/8] mm/hugetlb: retry the pool walk when the zonelist is rebuilt
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where a hugetlb fault bound to one node can take a pool page from another due to the rebuilding of the zonelist. The patch introduces a retry mechanism in the dequeue_hugetlb_folio_nodemask function, which checks if the zonelist has been rebuilt before using each zone returned by the walk. If the zonelist has changed, the function restarts the walk and resets the node it last tried to ensure that no nodes are skipped. This change is necessary because kprobes can hold the walk across the online process, leading to incorrect behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 7/8] mm/page_alloc: retry alloc_contig_pages() when the zonelist is rebuilt
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the alloc_contig_frozen_pages_noprof function to retry when the zonelist is rebuilt, which can cause a zone that was previously ineligible to become eligible. This change ensures that the function correctly handles changes to the zonelist and avoids allocating pages from zones that are not suitable for the requested allocation. The patch addresses an issue where the hugetlb pool walk could put gigantic pages in ZONE_MOVABLE, which is excluded by a previous commit. The change improves the reliability of memory allocation under certain conditions, such as when kprobes hold the walk across the online process.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 8/8] mm/page_alloc: keep a zone's pagesets when it goes empty
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the freeing of a zone's pagesets when it goes empty, which can lead to memory corruption and leaks. The pagesets are kept for the life of the zone, similar to pgdat->per_cpu_nodestats. This change is necessary because setup_zone_pageset() reuses existing pagesets and zone_pcp_init() keeps them when a node is re-added. The patch fixes a bug introduced by commit 340175b7d14d and addresses issues with memory allocation and deallocation in the presence of kprobes and cond_resched().

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses eight race conditions between memory hotplug and the Linux allocator, which can lead to failed allocations, NULL dereferences, or incorrect placement of pages. The races occur because zonelists are reordered in-place at runtime during hotplug, causing narrow but determinable windows for failure. The patches use a kprobe reproduction module to make these conditions deterministic and fix the issues by synchronizing access to zonelists and preferred zones.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/6] daxctl: online whole-device memory atomically when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the daxctl device control tool to online whole-device memory atomically when available, rather than onlining each block individually. This approach avoids racing issues with other agents that may be online blocks as they appear. The kernel only onlines from an 'unplugged' state, and if this fails (e.g., due to lack of hotremove support), the device is left unchanged and onlined per-block. The patch also updates the per-block path to fail when a device has no memory blocks, rather than reporting zero sections already online.

review_comments.author: Alison Schofield
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that using DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE in the atomic --no-movable path could place memory in ZONE_MOVABLE despite --no-movable, and suggested either changing it to DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE_KERNEL or adding a zone check

Reviewer noted that a reconfigure-device command may add memory twice, first offline at probe and then daxctl unplugs it and adds it back online, leaving the device unplugged if the re-add fails. Alison suggested transitioning directly from offline to an online state instead of falling back to per-block onlining.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Greg, 

A couple of things here...

The atomic --no-movable path uses DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE, leaving zone selection
to the kernel. With memory_hotplug.online_policy=auto-movable, IIUC this could
place memory in ZONE_MOVABLE despite --no-movable.

The per-block path checks the resulting zone and fails if it isn't ZONE_NORMAL,
but the atomic path skips that check.

Should this use DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE_KERNEL instead, or retain DAXCTL_KMEM_ONLINE
and add the same zone check?

---

With this, a "reconfigure-device -m system-ram" may add the memory twice.
First kmem adds it offline at probe and then daxctl unplugs it and adds it
back online. If that re-add fails, the device is left unplugged rather than
offline.

I get that falling back to per-block onlining would reopen the race this
series is addressing. Could the kernel interface support transitioning
directly from offline to an online state instead? It seems that would avoid
both the extra hotplug work and the left-unplugged failure case.

-- Alison

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/6] daxctl: offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds the ability to offline whole-device memory via atomic unplug when available, using the daxctl utility. When the kernel provides a 'daxX.Y/state' interface, writing 'unplugged' will atomically offload and remove the device's memory blocks. If all memory is already offline, the operation is still attempted but considered best effort. The patch also updates the 'daxctl list' command to omit 'movable' for devices with no blocks, and removes sysfs directories when unplugging a node's last memory block.

review_comments.author: Alison Schofield
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Alison Schofield noted that the patch changes the behavior of 'daxctl offline-memory' to remove memory blocks entirely, instead of leaving them present but offline, and requested that it keep its existing behavior unless reconfiguring the device.

Reviewer pointed out a potential race condition where another agent could online a block between the check and unplug, suggesting documentation of this edge case for users.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Greg,

I see you called this out in the cover letter, and that the kernel is
deliberately combining offlining and removing memory to avoid the race
before unbind.

But, this does change the behavior of the command "daxctl offline-memory".
Previously it left memory blocks present but offline and now it removes
them entirely.

Should offline-memory keep its existing behavior of leaving memory blocks
offline, and use atomic unplug only when reconfiguring the device?

---

When num_on == 0, another agent could online a block between the earlier
check and the unplug and that memory would then be removed.

I see this noted in the commit message. Is that worth documenting for
users?


-- Alison

Hi Greg,

Please change how the tests handle the absence of the new sysfs attribute.
If a test expects the new interface, a missing attribute should cause
the test to fail, with a clear error message. We have had problems in
the past with tests silently not executing letting defects go undetected.

Note that we don't require backward compatibility for the unit tests.
The utilities must continue working with older kernels, but tests for new
functionality should fail loudly when that functionality is missing.
(I'm aware that not all tests follow that guideline, and they need fixing.)

Please also leave the existing test cases as they were and run the new
state-dependent cases last.

A few stale state cases would exercise daxctl behavior that the kernel
selftest can't cover - 

  - Offline one memory block out-of-band, verify that daxctl list
    reports hotplug_state "inconsistent", then verify that
    offline-memory still leaves the device unplugged with its blocks
    removed.

  - Offline all blocks out-of-band, then verify that

  - With all blocks offline but the device state still reporting

are gone from /sys/devices/system/memory.  ie verify in sysfs directly
independent of the libdaxctl code being tested.

I found that libdaxctl undercounts memory blocks on multi-range devices.
I'm posting a separate fix and test for that. Nothing in this series needs
to change. I'll cc you for review.

Our ndctl emulation can't exercise multi-range hotplug, but the kernel

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel to unqueue deferred split folios outside of the lruvec lock, which is currently held in various paths such as move_folios_to_lru() and folio_batch_move_lru(). The lruvec lock protects the folio's LRU list and reclaim lists, but the deferred split queue lives on a separate list_lru with its own per-memcg per-node lock. series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths. This makes it easier to follow the code, especially after making page_counter_try_charge stock-aware. The change does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient management of memory usage. The change affects how memory and swap counters interact, potentially causing temporary divergence in their raw values. To maintain compatibility, the patch introduces a new logic to ensure that reclaim doesn't swap when memory fails first, even if memory and swap have equal limits. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. The change sets the stage for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles charge, refill, and hotplug operations for both stocks. If memory charge fails, only nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. The patch also preserves the user-visible cgroup-v1 memory invariant by reporting memory.usage_in_bytes as the smaller raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock management from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is necessary for future work on scalable and performant page_counters, such as the tiered memcg limits series. The patch preserves the invariant that memory.usage_in_bytes is less than or equal to memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes in cgroup v1, by reporting memory.usage_in_bytes as the smaller of the raw memory and memsw values. This change has no functional impact on memcg v2 users but does affect memcg v1 users by decoupling the memsw and memory stock management.

> local_trylock() takes a per-CPU
> spinlock, which is an rcu read
> lock along with migrate_disable
> 
> drain_stock
> css_put drops the last reference
> release work is queued
> 
> kworker runs css_release_work_fn()
> call_rcu() starts grace period G
> which waits for the refill task.
> 
> <preempt>
> drain_all_stock
> is_memcg_drain_needed()
> enters rcu_read_lock(), but
> grace period G does not wait
> since it started after G did
> 
> <prempt>
> 
> stock->cached[i] is cleared and
> unlocks. Grace period G ends,
> old is freed
> 
> mem_cgroup_is_descendant() reads
> old->css.cgroup which has just
> been freed.
> 
> To close this gap on PREEMPT_RT, switch the order of the referene drop
> and the publishing so that we publish the NULL pointer before dropping
> the reference. Note that this can only happen from drain_stock who can
> hold the last reference, but not on consume_stock since another
> reference will always be held. But fix this in both sites to maintain
> consistency.

> issue in my page_counter_stock series [1].

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 01/18] mm: free PG_rcu_free folios only after an RCU grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new page flag called PG_rcu_free to allow folios to be freed only after an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. This is necessary because without a reference, a folio can be freed while still being read by another CPU, leading to memory reuse issues. The patch adds support for this flag in various kernel files and introduces a new workqueue to handle the freeing of folios with this flag. It also includes a new counter in /proc/vmstat to track deferred pages. This patch is part of a larger series that aims to improve page management and reduce memory contention on large machines.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 02/18] splice: don't steal page cache folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's splice functionality to prevent it from stealing page cache folios, which are being reused without proper freeing. The patch removes the ->try_steal function from page_cache_pipe_buf_ops and instead copies the data when splicing from the page cache into a fuse file or virtio console. This change ensures that page cache memory is properly released after use, preventing potential issues with disk block reuse and file system corruption.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 03/18] fuse: don't move a folio with PG_rcu_free into a fuse file
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents a folio marked for RCU freeing from being moved into a fuse file, which can lead to unexpected behavior when the folio is still being copied by a lockless page cache read. The issue arises when a mapped file page is gifted with vmsplice(SPLICE_F_GIFT) and its file is then truncated. Instead of moving the folio, the patch copies it as fuse does in similar situations.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 04/18] mm: count the pages waiting for a grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new counter to track pages waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. These pages have a refcount of zero and are not on the free lists, making them invisible to existing counters. The new counter, NR_FREE_RCU_PAGES, is added to the /proc/vmstat output and show_free_areas() function. This change prepares for freeing these waiting pages sooner when they hold back needed memory.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 05/18] mm: expedite the grace period when a CPU has many deferred frees
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of deferred frees in the Linux kernel by introducing an expedited grace period when a CPU has many pending frees. When more than 4 MiB is pending on a CPU, the patch takes both lists and frees them after an expedited grace period, which interrupts every CPU. This approach aims to reduce memory pressure by freeing up memory quickly when it's needed most, such as when the zone is below its high watermark or when pages waiting in it are more than an eighth of its free pages. The patch also adds a new counter pgfree_rcu_expedite in /proc/vmstat to track the number of expedited runs that freed something.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 06/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before OOM
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to free pages waiting for a grace period before triggering an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer. When reclaiming fails, it checks if freeing these pages would bring an eligible zone above its minimum watermark, and if so, frees them and retries the allocation. This approach is designed to reduce the likelihood of OOM kills by attempting to free memory from pages that are waiting for a grace period before resorting to more drastic measures. The patch also introduces a new metric, pgfree_rcu_drain, to track the number of times this optimization occurs.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 07/18] mm: free the pages waiting for a grace period before isolation fails
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where the Linux kernel fails to allocate memory due to pages waiting for a grace period after migration. The issue arises when alloc_contig_range() and offline_pages() migrate folios out of a range, but some pages are still waiting for a grace period. To resolve this, the patch introduces a new function rcu_free_sync(), which frees every waiting folio, including those taken off the lists by a work. This allows the kernel to retry memory allocation after freeing the waiting pages. The approach taken is to add a check in offline_pages() to free waiting pages before retrying memory allocation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 08/18] mm/memory-failure: handle folios with PG_rcu_free
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where memory_failure() and soft_offline_page() cannot handle pages that are waiting for an RCU (Read-Copy-Update) grace period, which can lead to a poisoned page being handed out again. The patch introduces a new function mf_free_rcu_pages() that frees these waiting pages before handling the memory failure. It also ensures that the caller waits for a grace period after setting PG_hwpoison on the page to prevent readers from accessing the poisoned page. This approach prevents errors and ensures data integrity.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 09/18] mm: have folio_mark_accessed() return whether the folio is hot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `folio_mark_accessed()` function to return a boolean indicating whether the folio is considered 'hot' by the LRU (Least Recently Used) cache. A hot folio is one that has been recently accessed and is unlikely to be evicted from memory. The change prepares for future functionality where the caller can read the folios marked as hot without needing a reference to them. The patch also updates the function signature to return a boolean value instead of void.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 10/18] mm/filemap: mark a folio accessed in one place in filemap_read()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the filemap_read() function by removing duplicate calls to folio_mark_accessed(). It introduces a new helper function, filemap_read_accessed(), which marks a folio as accessed in one place. This change is intended to prepare for future decisions on which folios are worth reading without a reference. The patch does not alter the behavior of the filemap_read() function and only makes minor changes to its implementation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 11/18] mm/filemap: set PG_rcu_free on the folios that reads keep coming back to
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new flag, PG_rcu_free, which is set on folios that are frequently accessed by readers. The flag delays the free of these folios' memory for a grace period after they are freed, allowing readers to access them without holding a reference. This trade-off is only made for hot folios, and not for streaming reads or truncated files that are not frequently accessed. The patch also introduces a new field in /proc/vmstat to count the number of pages marked with this flag.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 12/18] mm/filemap: don't defer the free of folios of an inode being evicted
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the deferral of free operations for folios of an inode being evicted by clearing the PG_rcu_free flag when the final truncate removes a folio, especially in cases where the file is still open and under memory pressure or at umount. This ensures that no lockless reader can be in the page cache of an inode being evicted. The patch modifies the Linux kernel's mm/filemap.c and include/linux/page-flags.h files to achieve this goal.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 13/18] mm/filemap: store the end of a read in f_ra only when it changes
series_items.patch_summary: The patch proposes to optimize filemap_read() by storing the end of a read in f_ra.prev_pos only when it changes, reducing unnecessary writes to shared cache lines.

review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Identified a performance issue with the patch, pointing out that it's worse than useless and causes unnecessary writes to shared cache lines. Suggested replacing the patch with an alternative solution.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, 19 Oct 2026 at 05:50, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org> wrote:
>
> filemap_read() writes the end of every read to file->f_ra.prev_pos.
> Threads that read through one open file all write that cache line, on
> every read.  The value often stays the same, as for reads that start at
> the same offset each time.

This seems silly. That "often stays the same" is only true for the
pointless benchmark, no?

I don't think it's ever true in any real load.

            Linus

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged Linus' assessment, agreeing that the patch is bogus and causes performance issues. Announced plans to replace the patch with an alternative solution.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Oct 20, 2026 at 11:20:00AM -1000, Linus Torvalds wrote:
> On Mon, 19 Oct 2026 at 05:50, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org> wrote:
> >
> > filemap_read() writes the end of every read to file->f_ra.prev_pos.
> > Threads that read through one open file all write that cache line, on
> > every read.  The value often stays the same, as for reads that start at
> > the same offset each time.
> 
> This seems silly. That "often stays the same" is only true for the
> pointless benchmark, no?
> 
> I don't think it's ever true in any real load.

Right. The patch is bogus, not only the commit message.

It is worse than useless: for random reads prev_pos changes every time,
so the compare reads the shared line and then writes it anyway.
Bisecting a RocksDB slowdown led here: with patches 1-12 it runs at base
speed, this one costs 4-5% at 16-64 threads.

The store itself does matter in a real load.  RocksDB threads pread()
through one fd per SST file, opened with POSIX_FADV_RANDOM.  With the
folio refcount gone, the prev_pos store on that shared struct file is
what they fight over next.

For an FMODE_RANDOM file nothing reads prev_pos but filemap_read()
itself: readahead is forced and returns before looking at it.  Skipping
the store there takes a small hot table at 64 threads from 10.7M to
14.1M Gets/s, against 12.5M with the series as posted.

I will replace this patch with that.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 14/18] mm/filemap: read from the page cache without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes small file reads by allowing the page cache to be accessed without taking a reference on the folio, reducing the overhead of reference counting and improving performance. It achieves this by copying data from folios that are about to be freed under RCU read lock protection, and leaving large or problematic folios to the slow path for handling. The patch also limits the amount of data copied in each section to 512 KiB and skips files that have never had a flagged folio or are writably mapped.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 15/18] mm/filemap: read large folios without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of large folios in the Linux kernel's filemap module. A large folio is one that spans multiple pages or none at all. The patch introduces two new functions: `filemap_read_rcu_size` and `filemap_read_rcu_copy`. These functions allow for efficient copying of data from a large folio without requiring a reference to the entire range, which can be expensive in terms of memory usage. The patch also includes optimizations for handling splits after checking the folio's order. This change aims to improve performance by reducing the number of checks and references required when dealing with large files.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 16/18] mm/shmem: count accesses to a folio the way filemap_read() does
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way access to shmem folios is counted, aligning it with how filemap_read() handles other files. Specifically, a read operation marks a folio as accessed unless it starts at the same position where the previous read ended. This change ensures that reads from the same bytes through one open file are only counted once, rather than each time they start at the beginning of the folio. Additionally, this patch sets PG_rcu_free on tmpfs folios that are repeatedly accessed and marks them as accessed even if a write operation is performed first.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 17/18] mm/shmem: read without folio references
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the shmem_file_read_iter function to avoid taking a reference on every folio it reads, which can cause bouncing of the refcount when small reads are made from multiple CPUs. Instead, it uses filemap_read_rcu to copy data without acquiring a reference, and continues with the existing loop where necessary. This change also drops the folio lock and reference, making reads non-atomic against writes or hole punches. Additionally, it ensures that readahead is not triggered on shmem folios, which have their PG_readahead bit set as PG_reclaim.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 18/18] mm/filemap: add a debugfs switch for lockless page cache reads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a debugfs switch called 'lockless_page_cache_read' that allows users to toggle lockless page cache reads on or off. When enabled, this feature defers the freeing of memory for hot pages by an RCU grace period, allowing for faster reads but potentially leading to memory leaks if not used carefully. The patch also includes a static key to keep the test off the read path and provides a way to turn off lockless page cache reads in case of issues or workloads that lose on this trade-off.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a new mechanism to read from the page cache without taking a reference on folios, which can lead to refcount bouncing between CPUs. The approach involves marking accessed folios as PG_rcu_free and deferring their free until an RCU grace period. This allows for more efficient handling of small reads and reduces the overhead of lock contention. The series includes 18 patches that implement this new mechanism in various parts of the Linux kernel, including filemap_read(), shmem, and memory_failure(). The goal is to improve performance on systems with many CPUs by reducing the number of references taken on folios and minimizing the impact of refcount bouncing.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about contention on the folio's reference count, explaining how PG_rcu_free flag avoids this issue by allowing reads to copy from folios without taking a reference and delaying their free until an RCU grace period. The author confirmed that the flag is only needed for large machines with 64-bit architectures.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Reading a page cache folio without taking a reference would keep CPUs
that read the same file from bouncing its refcount.  But without a
reference the folio can be freed, and its memory reused, while the
reader copies from it.

Add PG_rcu_free: the free of a folio with the flag waits for an RCU
grace period.  A reader that saw the flag under rcu_read_lock(), and
then still found the folio where it looked, can read it until
rcu_read_unlock().  A split copies the flag, as such a reader may still
be reading the new folios.

The folios wait on per-CPU lists, one grace period in flight per CPU:
call_rcu() per folio would queue a callback for every folio of a
truncated file.  A work, which can reschedule, frees each batch.
Reclaim depends on these frees, so the workqueue is WQ_MEM_RECLAIM.

The flag is 64-bit only (CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE): page flags are scarce
on 32-bit, and the contention this avoids is a problem of large
machines.

pgfree_rcu in /proc/vmstat counts the deferred pages.  Nothing sets the
flag yet.

+/*
+ * Each CPU has at most one grace period in flight (@queued), covering
+ * @batch.  Folios freed meanwhile wait on @pending for the next one.
+ */
+struct rcu_free_pcpu {
+	spinlock_t lock;
+	bool queued;
+	struct list_head pending;
+	struct list_head batch;
+	struct rcu_work rwork;
+};
+
+static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct rcu_free_pcpu, rcu_free_pcpu);
+
+static struct workqueue_struct *rcu_free_wq __ro_after_init;
+
+static void rcu_free_start(struct rcu_free_pcpu *r)
+{
+	lockdep_assert_held(&r->lock);
+
+	if (r->queued || list_empty(&r->pending))
+		return;
+
+	list_splice_init(&r->pending, &r->batch);
+	r->queued = true;
+	WARN_ON_ONCE(!queue_rcu_work(rcu_free_wq, &r->rwork));
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_pages(struct list_head *list)
+{
+	struct folio_batch fbatch;
+	struct folio *folio, *next;
+
+	folio_batch_init(&fbatch);
+	list_for_each_entry_safe(folio, next, list, lru) {
+		if (!folio_batch_add(&fbatch, folio)) {
+			free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+			cond_resched_tasks_rcu_qs();
+		}
+	}
+	if (folio_batch_count(&fbatch))
+		free_unref_folios(&fbatch);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_workfn(struct work_struct *work)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = container_of(to_rcu_work(work),
+					       struct rcu_free_pcpu, rwork);
+	LIST_HEAD(done);
+
+	spin_lock_irq(&r->lock);
+	list_splice_init(&r->batch, &done);
+	r->queued = false;
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irq(&r->lock);
+
+	rcu_free_pages(&done);
+}
+
+static void rcu_free_defer(struct folio *folio)
+{
+	struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = raw_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu);
+	unsigned long flags;
+
+	spin_lock_irqsave(&r->lock, flags);
+	list_add_tail(&folio->lru, &r->pending);
+	rcu_free_start(r);
+	spin_unlock_irqrestore(&r->lock, flags);
+}
+
+static void __init rcu_free_init(void)
+{
+	int cpu;
+
+	if (!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PAGE_RCU_FREE))
+		return;
+
+	rcu_free_wq = alloc_workqueue("rcu_free",
+				      WQ_MEM_RECLAIM | WQ_PERCPU, 0);
+
+	for_each_possible_cpu(cpu) {
+		struct rcu_free_pcpu *r = per_cpu_ptr(&rcu_free_pcpu, cpu);
+
+		spin_lock_init(&r->lock);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->pending);
+		INIT_LIST_HEAD(&r->batch);
+		INIT_RCU_WORK(&r->rwork, rcu_free_workfn);
+	}
+}

From: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

reused without being freed: remove_mapping() takes the folio out of the

From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
Subject: [PATCH v4] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

Since commit 7e8756d7ad22 ("mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim
storm in defrag_mode"), direct reclaim and compaction for non-movable
requests under defrag_mode run at pageblock_order, to produce the whole
blocks that ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT needs. The retry decisions that follow
still use the request order. An order-0 request can therefore retry
indefinitely without ever reaching the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT fallback:

- Reclaim at pageblock_order gives up after one pass as soon as a zone
  looks compaction_ready(), and do_try_to_free_pages() then returns 1
  even though nothing was reclaimed. It returns before the retry that
  would reclaim memory.low-protected cgroups, so when most memory is
  protected, the pass that did run finds next to nothing.

- Compaction at pageblock_order fails or is deferred.

- should_reclaim_retry() takes the reported progress as progress for
  the order-0 request and resets no_progress_loops. The request
  retries.

Order 1-3 requests loop the same way, and should_compact_retry() also
checks their pageblock_order compaction result against the request
order.

On a production host (64G, defrag_mode, memory.low covering most of the
workload), 95% of direct reclaim runs were order-9 runs that returned 1
with nothing reclaimed, at up to 60k runs per second. Across ~200M
should_reclaim_retry() calls in a day, no_progress_loops never left 0.
The spinning allocations were SLUB slab refills for inode and dentry
caches. The time spent registers as memory pressure, and pressure-based
OOM killing takes down both workloads and system services.

For promoted requests:

- Reclaim progress does not reset no_progress_loops, as for costly
  orders.

- should_compact_retry() checks the compaction result at the promoted
  order and does not retry COMPACT_SKIPPED, since the request can fall
  back. The compaction priority floor and the COMPACT_SUCCESS retry
  limit stay those of the request order, so a non-costly request still
  gets its COMPACT_PRIO_SYNC_FULL pass before it falls back.

When a promoted request takes the fallback, reset the retry counters,
so that the fallback attempt gets a full retry budget before the OOM
killer is considered. A request whose reclaim was not promoted spent
its budget on the request itself and keeps its counters, as Usama Arif
pointed out.

__alloc_pages_slowpath() computes the promoted order once per iteration
and keeps it in alloc_context for direct reclaim, direct compaction and
the two retry helpers, so no callee has to recompute it. Harry Yoo asked
for the promoted order to be explicit rather than derived in each
callee, and Vlastimil Babka suggested alloc_context over new function
parameters.

In a VM reproducer (32G, defrag_mode, inode churn under memory.low):

                                        before    after
    should_reclaim_retry() calls           63M     293k
    peak memory pressure (PSI some avg10)  99%      12%

File creation runs 5.7x faster.

Fixes: 7e8756d7ad22 ("mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim storm in defrag_mode")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Assisted-by: LLM
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
---
v4:
 - keep the promoted order in alloc_context instead of passing it as a
   new parameter (Vlastimil Babka)

 mm/page_alloc.c | 65 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++--------------------
 mm/page_alloc.h |  2 ++
 2 files changed, 41 insertions(+), 26 deletions(-)

diff --git a/mm/page_alloc.c b/mm/page_alloc.c
index 12fac9084c48..c593913a14f8 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -4127,6 +4127,12 @@ __alloc_pages_may_oom(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	return page;
 }
 
+static inline bool order_nofrag_promoted(unsigned int order,
+					 const struct alloc_context *ac)
+{
+	return ac->reclaim_compact_order != order;
+}
+
 /*
  * Maximum number of compaction retries with a progress before OOM
  * killer is consider as the only way to move forward.
@@ -4149,22 +4155,7 @@ __alloc_pages_direct_compact(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 		.order = order,
 		.page = NULL,
 	};
-	int compact_order = order;
-
-	/*
-	 * If fallbacks are not permitted (defrag_mode), we either
-	 * need to reclaim space in a block of matching type, or clear
-	 * out an entire block to allow __rmqueue_claim() to convert.
-	 *
-	 * Reclaim by itself is primarily freeing space in movable
-	 * blocks, since that's where the LRU pages live. So this
-	 * works for movable requests, but not for others.
-	 *
-	 * For those, promote the order to help make blocks, instead
-	 * of spinning in reclaim alone unproductively.
-	 */
-	if ((alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT) && ac->migratetype != MIGRATE_MOVABLE)
-		compact_order = max(order, pageblock_order);
+	int compact_order = ac->reclaim_compact_order;
 
 	if (!compact_order)
 		return NULL;
@@ -4257,7 +4248,7 @@ should_compact_retry(gfp_t gfp_mask, struct alloc_context *ac, int order,
 	int retries = *compaction_retries;
 	enum compact_priority priority = *compact_priority;
 
-	if (!order)
+	if (!ac->reclaim_compact_order)
 		return false;
 
 	if (fatal_signal_pending(current))
@@ -4266,10 +4257,12 @@ should_compact_retry(gfp_t gfp_mask, struct alloc_context *ac, int order,
 	/*
 	 * Compaction was skipped due to a lack of free order-0
 	 * migration targets. Continue if reclaim can help.
+	 * Promoted requests fall back instead.
 	 */
 	if (compact_result == COMPACT_SKIPPED) {
-		ret = compaction_zonelist_suitable(ac, order, alloc_flags,
-						   gfp_mask);
+		if (!order_nofrag_promoted(order, ac))
+			ret = compaction_zonelist_suitable(ac, order,
+							   alloc_flags, gfp_mask);
 		goto out;
 	}
 
@@ -4468,11 +4461,7 @@ __alloc_pages_direct_reclaim(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	struct page *page = NULL;
 	unsigned long pflags;
 	bool drained = false;
-	int reclaim_order = order;
-
-	/* Match the slowpath compaction promotion in __alloc_pages_direct_compact */
-	if ((alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT) && ac->migratetype != MIGRATE_MOVABLE)
-		reclaim_order = max(order, pageblock_order);
+	int reclaim_order = ac->reclaim_compact_order;
 
 	psi_memstall_enter(&pflags);
 	*did_some_progress = __perform_reclaim(gfp_mask, reclaim_order, ac);
@@ -4648,9 +4637,12 @@ should_reclaim_retry(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned order,
 	/*
 	 * Costly allocations might have made a progress but this doesn't mean
 	 * their order will become available due to high fragmentation so
-	 * always increment the no progress counter for them
+	 * always increment the no progress counter for them. The same goes for
+	 * promoted requests: their reclaim reports progress when it backs off
+	 * for compaction without freeing anything.
 	 */
-	if (did_some_progress && order <= PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER)
+	if (did_some_progress && order <= PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER &&
+	    !order_nofrag_promoted(order, ac))
 		*no_progress_loops = 0;
 	else
 		(*no_progress_loops)++;
@@ -4934,6 +4926,22 @@ __alloc_pages_slowpath(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	/* If allocation has taken excessively long, warn about it */
 	check_alloc_stall_warn(gfp_mask, ac->nodemask, order, alloc_start_time);
 
+	/*
+	 * If fallbacks are not permitted (defrag_mode), we either
+	 * need to reclaim space in a block of matching type, or clear
+	 * out an entire block to allow __rmqueue_claim() to convert.
+	 *
+	 * Reclaim by itself is primarily freeing space in movable
+	 * blocks, since that's where the LRU pages live. So this
+	 * works for movable requests, but not for others.
+	 *
+	 * For those, promote the order to help make blocks, instead
+	 * of spinning in reclaim alone unproductively.
+	 */
+	ac->reclaim_compact_order = order;
+	if ((alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT) && ac->migratetype != MIGRATE_MOVABLE)
+		ac->reclaim_compact_order = max(order, pageblock_order);
+
 	/* Try direct reclaim and then allocating */
 	if (!compact_first) {
 		page = __alloc_pages_direct_reclaim(gfp_mask, order, alloc_flags,
@@ -5015,6 +5023,11 @@ __alloc_pages_slowpath(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	/* Reclaim/compaction failed to prevent the fallback */
 	if (defrag_mode && (alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT)) {
 		alloc_flags &= ~ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT;
+		/* Retries went into making blocks, start the fallback afresh */
+		if (order_nofrag_promoted(order, ac)) {
+			no_progress_loops = 0;
+			compaction_retries = 0;
+		}
 		goto retry;
 	}
 
diff --git a/mm/page_alloc.h b/mm/page_alloc.h
index b9259deddb59..2b1017a91928 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.h
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.h
@@ -93,6 +93,8 @@ struct alloc_context {
 	bool spread_dirty_pages;
 	/* Only flags that are global to the whole allocation go here. */
 	unsigned int alloc_flags;
+	/* Set by __alloc_pages_slowpath() before reclaim and compaction */
+	unsigned int reclaim_compact_order;
 };

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain expressed concern that defrag mode may not improve mTHP allocation success, citing a synthetic benchmark where it caused warn_alloc and compact_stalls to occur more frequently than without defrag mode.
review_comments.raw_body:
AFAIU defrag mode is not going to improve mTHP allocation success.

I ran a synthetic benchmark faulting in lots of 64k mTHP with swap enabled,
defrag mode caused me to enter a warn_alloc (and 8 times more compact_stalls),
which didn't happen without defrag.

So perhaps bundle the default with pageblock_order eagerness etc.
